title: Material consumption is rising faster than ecological capacity, with high-income demand and built-environment systems driving unequal impacts
source_unit: UNEP-hosted International Resource Panel Global Resources Outlook 2024
geography: Global; resource-use, material-footprint, income-group, regional, sectoral, and scenario comparisons as specified by the report

observations.period: 1970-2024 historical material-use trend summarized in Global Resources Outlook 2024

denominator.unit: metric tonnes of global material extraction in 2024

global_material_extraction.unit: billion tonnes in 2024, up from 30 billion tonnes in 1970

per_capita_material_demand.unit: tonnes per person in 2024, up from 8.4 tonnes in 1970

high_income_vs_low_income_resource_use.unit: times: material consumption rate in high-income countries compared with low-income countries

built_environment_mobility_food_energy_s.unit: percent approximate share of global material demand attributed collectively to built environment, mobility, food, and energy

asia_pacific_consumption_share.unit: percent approximate share of global material consumption attributed to Asia and the Pacific by 2017

observations.method: International Resource Panel assessment of material extraction, domestic material consumption, material footprints, trade, sectoral drivers, productivity, waste, emissions, and inequality across historical global data.
observations.uncertainty: Material extraction, consumption, and footprint measures capture different stages and responsibility allocations; regional shares and income-group ratios should not be read as household consumption or direct causal climate impacts. Historical estimates depend on national accounts, trade data, and modeling assumptions.
observations.subgroup: High-, upper-middle-, lower-middle-, and low-income countries; regions, sectors, producers, consumers, infrastructure systems, and populations exposed to resource extraction and environmental impacts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising material use has accompanied poverty reduction and infrastructure build-out. Higher resource use does not automatically imply wasteful consumption, and efficiency or circularity can alter the link between material demand, welfare, and environmental pressure.

historical_trends_resource_extraction_20.unit: index relative to 2020 under the Historical Trends scenario, approximately 60% higher by 2060

historical_trends_primary_energy_2060.unit: index relative to 2020 under the Historical Trends scenario, approximately 50% higher by 2060

historical_trends_food_fibre_biomass_206.unit: index relative to 2020 under the Historical Trends scenario, approximately 80% higher by 2060

historical_trends_net_greenhouse_gas_emi.unit: index relative to 2020 under the Historical Trends scenario, more than 20% higher by 2060

sustainability_transition_direction.value: resource pressures and environmental impacts fall below current levels while global inequalities decline

policy_route.value: resource productivity, circularity, sustainable provisioning, financial and trade incentives, and social equity

observations.method: UNEP/International Resource Panel scenario analysis comparing a Historical Trends pathway with a Sustainability Transition pathway across resource, energy, land, emissions, biodiversity, and inequality indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Scenarios are conditional pathways, not forecasts; outcomes depend on policy implementation, technology, behavior, population, income, trade, and model assumptions. The index values do not identify who bears transition costs or whether services improve for a particular community.
observations.subgroup: Governments, firms, households, cities, infrastructure and mobility systems, food and energy sectors, workers, communities near extraction, and populations affected by climate and pollution.
observations.counterinterpretation: A sustainability-transition scenario can reduce aggregate pressure without guaranteeing local justice, affordability, labor protections, or equal access. Circularity and efficiency can also generate rebound effects if total consumption continues to grow.

related_sources.claim: UNEP summarizes the income-group resource-use and climate-impact inequality findings.
UNEP describes circularity, sustainable provisioning, and decoupling as policy routes.

boundary: This record adds a global resource-consumption, sectoral-demand, environmental-inequality, and transition-policy route. It does not measure household consumption, local extraction harm, causal climate effects, or the distributional incidence of a particular sustainability policy.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: UNEP Global Resources Outlook 2024 landing page, official International Resource Panel PDF, press materials, and scenario sections retrieved; historical extraction, per-capita demand, income-group ratio, sectoral share, regional shift, scenario indices, and policy caveats cross-checked against UNEP materials.
